title: In Praise Of Japan’s Failure To Keep Up | NOEMA
gist: Fitzpatrick argues that Japan's chronic failure to commercialize its own inventions (contactless payments, EVs, early AI) and its plodding, risk-averse institutions — now under pressure from a Silicon Valley-style startup push and US VC influx amid steep economic decline — may paradoxically position it to preserve social cohesion and 'technological sovereignty' against Western technological determinism.

insights.claim: Japan perfected contactless IC-card payment technology decades ago, but domestic distrust of anything but cash meant it gained a widespread local following only after the tech took off in Europe and elsewhere in the 2000s.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Domestic adoption friction can strand a technological lead; first-mover invention does not equal market capture.
insights.quote: the contactless technology perfected in Japan decades ago initially went nowhere
insights.locator: Yet this gaffe can be forgiven

insights.claim: Japan's research routinely fails to achieve global impact commensurate with its quality because it lacks the 'aggressive cultural machinery' (PR, business development, storytelling) to turn research into bankable international assets.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Japanese deep-tech IP may be undervalued/under-commercialized; value accrues to whoever packages and scales it.
insights.quote: What is missing, as is so often the case in Japan, is the aggressive cultural machinery required to turn raw research into a bankable international asset.
insights.locator: What is missing, as is so often

insights.claim: The most prestigious startup factory at Tokyo University has only one part-time PR representative, and she does not speak English, illustrating how communications are treated as peripheral.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: University spinouts lack go-to-market capacity; a gap for foreign partners/acquirers.
insights.quote: Even the most prestigious startup factory at Tokyo University has only one part-time PR rep. She does not speak English.

insights.claim: Japan pioneered commercial electric cars (Toyota, ~30 years ago), self-driving vehicles and early AI/machine learning, yet less cautious neighbors ran with the tech and Japan now finds it 'overslept' in all these fields.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Pattern of Japanese pioneering then ceding scale to faster adopters (China, US) — watch for repeats in robotics.
insights.locator: It was Toyota that ushered me

insights.claim: China may have gained its lead by 'distilling' ideas from Japan and elsewhere, but it now outpaces others through the speed at which it puts applications to use.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Deployment speed, not invention, is the competitive moat in applied tech.

insights.claim: The 'Galápagos' theory holds that Japan's tech standards and business practices evolved a unique character incompatible with overseas demand, so startups gain domestic fans but face a 'death march' abroad due to weak language skills, overengineering and poor marketing.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Japanese consumer-tech exports structurally disadvantaged; domestic-only champions.

insights.claim: Former Apple director Hideki Onda attributes Japan's 'superficially hi-tech' Galápagos evolution to its deeply cautious, conservative business and political classes, a poor fit for ruthless startup capitalism.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Institutional conservatism is the binding constraint on Japanese disruption.

insights.claim: In the 1980s Japanese scientists were diving deep into artificial neurons and machine learning while Western researchers were skeptical of neural networks; AI researcher Yutaka Matsuo says Japan was ahead then 'but perhaps that doesn’t mean a lot now.'
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Early research leads in AI did not translate into today's AI industry position.
insights.quote: “We say Japan was ahead at the time,” AI researcher Yutaka Matsuo told me. “But perhaps that doesn’t mean a lot now.”

insights.claim: Shuji Nakamura, inventor of the white LED, was originally rewarded with a corporate bonus of just 20,000 yen (about $200), exemplifying how Japan's corporate system mistreats innovators.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Weak inventor incentives drive talent emigration from Japanese corporates.

themes.theme: Japan's push to import the Silicon Valley model

insights.claim: Japan's AI regulations have been made as loose as those in the U.S., which many see as an incentive for American corporations to move in.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Light-touch Japanese AI rules may attract US AI/cloud investment into Japan.
insights.locator: There is still an unfulfilled desire

insights.claim: Peter Thiel's trade mission was cheerfully received in Tokyo by premier Sanae Takaichi, and Marc Andreessen opened his firm's first overseas office in Japan this summer, signaling U.S. venture capital arriving fast.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: US VC inflows into Japan accelerating; watch deal flow and exits on Tokyo markets.
insights.quote: Marc Andreessen , boss of one of the heftiest firms, opened his first overseas office in Japan this summer.

insights.claim: Japan now sees the Silicon Valley model as the one that might get it out of its economic hole, with Tokyo desperate for more startups and more 'successful exits.'
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Policy tailwinds for startup ecosystem, IPOs and VC in Japan.
insights.quote: It is no secret that Japan now sees the Silicon Valley model as the one that might get it out of its considerable hole.

insights.claim: Brandon Hill argues Japan should go beyond creating more startups and focus on creating more globally competitive companies.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Quality of scale-ups, not count of startups, is the metric to track.
insights.locator: But Japan should be thinking beyond

insights.claim: The author argues university-linked founders take grants for 'global startups' while skipping the global part since most don't speak English, making the 'be global from the start' requirement a sham.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Government startup subsidies may be producing low-quality, domestically-bound firms.
insights.quote: No slogan has ever been emptier than “be global from the start,” as most of these founders don’t speak English.

insights.claim: Japanese universities — slow and hierarchical — repurpose poorly as startup incubators, which must be fast and unstable, producing an 'almighty clash of civilizations' under current policy.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Skepticism warranted toward university-spinout-driven growth plans.
insights.locator: But instead of impacting our world

insights.claim: Many government-funded university efforts focus on Japan's stockpile of zombie enterprises kept alive by cheap credit and handouts rather than global market performance.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Zombie-firm overhang continues to misallocate capital in Japan.
insights.locator: But appealing fictions have a habit

insights.claim: The Economist suggests Tokyo's 'startups first' growth plan looks woefully misguided, as Japan's corporate culture favors conformism, generalists and risk-aversion, so monetizing innovation will remain a struggle.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Expect underwhelming returns from Japan's startup push.

insights.claim: In critical fields like AI, semiconductors and defense tech, the author says Japan's chance to lead has already 'sailed away' with its frustrated emigre innovators.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Discount Japanese leadership claims in AI/semis; talent flight matters.

insights.claim: Japan's nominal GDP fell from second in the world to third in 2010 and fourth in 2023, and its share of global nominal GDP dropped from about 18% in 1995 to about 3.8% in 2025.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Scale of Japan's relative economic decline frames policy desperation.
insights.quote: The country’s share of global nominal GDP has fallen sharply, from approximately 18% in 1995 to approximately 3.8% in 2025.
insights.locator: The country’s economic emergency is real

insights.claim: Japan's nominal GDP per capita has fallen from second in the world to 38th, real wages have stagnated for 30 years, and the yen is at a low not seen for nearly 40 years.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Weak yen and stagnant wages sustain pressure for structural reform and foreign capital entry.
insights.quote: Real wages have stagnated for 30 years; the yen has fallen to a low not seen for nearly 40 years.
insights.locator: The country’s economic emergency is real

insights.claim: The 1991 collapse of the 1980s boom created a fear of risk-taking and retreat into safe jobs, investments and governments; a 2024 Bank of Japan survey found many firms curbed investment and built cash reserves after the crisis and later shocks.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Corporate cash hoarding is an entrenched behavior — a lever for governance/activist plays.

insights.claim: Japan has the ingredients of a supreme techno-state — elite scientists, a 'magic-money spigot' of quantitative easing and near-zero rates, and world-class manufacturing — but lacks the recipe.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Capital availability isn't the bottleneck; execution and institutions are.
insights.locator: But there are reasons for hope

insights.claim: Livedoor's 2005 hostile bid for Nippon Broadcasting (buying 29.6% in off-hours trading to approach a third) prompted a law change extending takeover rules to off-hours trading; founder Takefumi Horie was later jailed ~21 months for falsifying results (reported ~5bn yen pretax profit vs an actual ~300m yen loss).
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Japan historically punishes aggressive Anglo-Saxon capital tactics; regulatory backlash risk for disruptors.
insights.locator: Horie’s style put him at the center

insights.claim: The Horie case signaled to Japan's startup community that non-consensus, Anglo-Saxon capitalism would be punished, causing aspiring 'tall poppy' startups to retreat and effectively canceling the startup revolution of that era.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Cultural/legal precedents shape founder risk appetite for a generation.

insights.claim: The author's contrarian thesis is that Japan's slow, plodding institutions may have helped it dodge a bullet, giving it room to install 'rugged technological sovereignty' and escape the technological determinism infecting the West.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Japan as a potential model/market for slower, regulated tech adoption and sovereignty-focused tech.
insights.quote: Japan’s plodding ways and institutions incompatible with hyper-capitalism offer a chance to install some kind of rugged technological sovereignty.

insights.claim: In 1996 Japan's education minister refused Apple's push to bring its teaching tech to schools; 30 years on, the author sees 'method in the minister’s madness' as screen-based learning proves no silver bullet.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: EdTech skepticism gaining legitimacy globally.
insights.locator: To best illustrate this, Onda recalled

insights.claim: After a drop in student literacy, Sweden reversed its push toward digital learning, banned cellphones in schools, and returned to paper textbooks.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Policy reversal on digital learning benefits print textbook publishers; headwind for edtech.
insights.quote: Cellphones have been banned in schools, and the textbook industry rejoices at schools’ return to paper.
insights.locator: After noting a drop in student

insights.claim: A Japanese tech journalist argues Silicon Valley is optimized to maximize returns rather than human wellbeing, and expects a culture clash 'of Titanic proportions' as U.S. tech pushes into Japan.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Expect social/regulatory friction for US platforms in Japan.
insights.quote: “Ultimately, Silicon Valley is not primarily optimized to maximize human wellbeing. It is optimized to maximize returns.”

insights.claim: In a 2006 Japanese government survey, nearly 70% of Japanese companies said employees were important stakeholders and 90% planned to maintain long-term employment.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Stakeholder capitalism norms limit lean-restructuring upside in Japanese equities.

insights.claim: Japan's overemployment-oriented labor policies function as a 'massive job creation scheme' that American-style lean capitalism would threaten; this caution has preserved livelihoods.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Automation/AI adoption in Japan likely to be slowed by labor-protection priorities.
insights.quote: As outdated and sluggish as the nation’s institutions might be, their limbic caution has preserved livelihoods.

insights.claim: The journalist argues responsibility now lies with long-tradition countries like those in Europe and Japan to propose socially responsible uses of technology, echoing Japan's nascent call for 'technological sovereignty' and efforts to reduce dependency on U.S. tech.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Tech-sovereignty agendas could create demand for non-US tech vendors.

insights.claim: The author frames the U.S.-led tech alliance 'Pax Silica' as a shotgun wedding whose vow is: join our techno view of the world or be made irrelevant by it.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Allied tech-bloc alignment pressures smaller states into US tech dependency.
insights.quote: The vow is simple: Join our techno view of the world or be made irrelevant by it.

insights.claim: In 2021 UNESCO called for human oversight of AI and a basis for societies to accept or reject AI systems; the author argues societies should decide which technologies to adopt, how fast, and for whose benefit.
insights.speaker: MICHAEL FITZPATRICK
insights.so_what: Rising regulatory push for societal consent over AI deployment.
